paper_context.research_question: How should word embeddings be evaluated so that evaluation reflects their usefulness for transfer learning, particularly in terms of data efficiency and simple supervised tasks?
contribution_style: proposal of evaluation protocol (vary training set size, report learning curves/AUC)
empirical comparison of multiple pretrained embeddings across tasks and model classes
practical recommendations for including supervised, simple tasks and diverse classifiers
main_claims: Current popular evaluation practices for word embeddings (especially unsupervised intrinsic measures like cosine-based similarity and constant-model analogy tests) do not adequately reflect how useful embeddings are for transfer learning.
Evaluation should emphasize data efficiency (report performance across varying training set sizes) and simple supervised tasks to measure how easily useful information can be extracted.
Including learnable (supervised) versions of similarity and analogy benchmarks yields additional insights and can improve performance over constant/unsupervised baselines.
Ranking of embeddings changes as available supervised data size varies; data-efficiency properties differ across embeddings and tasks.
Some embeddings encode information nonlinearly (so nonlinear models can outperform linear ones), which questions relying solely on linear/cosine-based evaluations.
Simple single-word properties (POS, sentiment) tend to be quickly recoverable with small data, while higher-order relations (analogy) are harder and benefit from supervised learning.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: data efficiency: learning curves across varying training set sizes and AUC of those curves
task simplicity/type: performance on simple supervised tasks (single-word classification, sentence classification) and supervised versions of similarity/analogy
model class diversity: comparing linear vs nonlinear classifiers (and constant baselines) to detect nonlinear encoding
robustness/stability: changes in embedding ranking between small-data and large-data regimes
generalization: cross-dataset/task variability and statistical significance of rank differences (e.g., ANOVA-based testing)
practical applicability: how quickly downstream models reach acceptable performance (sample complexity)

extracted_claims.claim_label: Evaluation should focus on data efficiency
extracted_claims.claim_text: Evaluation should emphasize data efficiency: vary available supervised training set size, report learning curves and aggregate measures (e.g., AUC) to reflect how quickly useful information can be extracted from embeddings.

uncertainty_flags: Choice of aggregation metric (AUC) proposed as sensible default but alternative aggregations or weighting across dataset sizes are not compared.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Including learnable (supervised) versions of similarity and analogy benchmarks yields additional insights and can substantially improve absolute performance compared to constant/unsupervised baselines.
evidence: §3.4: "For solving Analogy we implemented a shallow neural network... we were able to improve absolute score upon the tested subset on average by absolute 11%".
§3.4: "In the case of Similarity dataset the best performing model was Support Vector Regression... similarly as in Analogy datasets we also improve over the constant models."
Figure 2 and Figure 4 present supervised-vs-constant comparisons for SimLex and WordRep subsets.
uncertainty_flags: Improvements reported for tested datasets/models; generality to other analogy/similarity sets and choices of supervised model hyperparameters is not fully explored.
Magnitude of improvement varies by dataset and embedding; not all datasets show large gains (some constant baselines already near chance or high).

extracted_claims.claim_label: Embedding rankings change with data size
extracted_claims.claim_text: Ranking of embeddings changes as available supervised data size varies; data-efficiency properties differ across embeddings and tasks, producing nontrivial rank changes between early (small-data) and late (large-data) points on learning curves.
evidence: §3.5: "Mean absolute value of change of ranking is approximately ... 0.6 ... which means that usually an embeddings has a changed rank after training".
Table 1 and Table 3 show ranks at 30% vs 100% splits and AUC-based rank; commentary that some embeddings move up/down.
Figure 3 visualizes rank at beginning and end of learning across categories.
uncertainty_flags: The reported average rank change (0.6) is relatively small; interpretation depends on the ranking method (ANOVA-based grouping) and dataset/task aggregation.
Stability measures depend on the set of tasks and embeddings evaluated; other embeddings or task selections might yield different behavior.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Some embeddings encode information nonlinearly (so nonlinear models can outperform linear ones), indicating that relying solely on linear/cosine-based evaluations can miss extractable information.
evidence: Abstract: "information ... tends to be non–linearly encoded in the embedding space".
§3.6: "More specifically, are there embeddings especially fitted for use with linear models? Clearly some embeddings in fact are, see Fig. 1."
Figure 1: normalized difference between best nonlinear and best linear model per embedding; descriptive text explaining GloVe100 vs GloVe300 nonlinear behavior.
uncertainty_flags: The degree to which nonlinear models outperform linear ones is task- and embedding-dependent; some cases show small differences.
The selection of nonlinear model classes (RF, RBF-SVM, CNN, small NN) constrains the interpretation of 'nonlinear encoding'.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Simple single-word properties (POS, sentiment, color, synset membership) tend to be quickly recoverable with small amounts of supervised data and fitting adds little benefit over constant/linear baselines.
evidence: §3.5: "rank change after training on full dataset is relatively low for Single word datasets... simple information about words ... is always quickly accessible".
Table 3: ranks at 30% and 100% splits for Single word datasets showing small changes.
§3.7: "For Analogy tasks achieved accuracy scores are below 25%, whereas in the case of Single word average accuracy is around 80% (and fitting classifier adds on average only 2%)."
uncertainty_flags: Single-word datasets used are derived from specific lexicons; results may not generalize to other single-word properties or rarer labels.
Exact sample sizes and class imbalance effects per single-word dataset are not fully detailed in the extraction; these affect 'quickly recoverable' interpretation.

extracted_claims.claim_text: A recommended practical default for embedding evaluation is to report learning curves over varying dataset sizes, compute AUC of those curves per task, and include a diverse set of model classes (linear and nonlinear) and simple supervised tasks.
evidence: Proposal: "A sensible default is to report AUC of learning curve for each task, and pick set of tasks that are most interesting".
Proposal summary bullet points: focus on data efficiency, supervised simple tasks, and diverse set of models.
Conclusions reiterate inclusion of data efficiency metrics and model diversity.
uncertainty_flags: Recommendation given as "sensible default" but no formal comparison to alternatives (e.g., specific curve aggregation, statistical tests across AUC) is provided.
Computational and reproducibility costs of running many model classes and repeated splits are not quantified.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Learnable analogy neural regressor improves over 3COSADD
extracted_claims.claim_text: A trainable regression neural network for analogy (initialized to reproduce 3COSADD) can improve analogy accuracy substantially on WordRep subsets (average absolute improvement ~11%).

uncertainty_flags: Reported improvement is on tested subset(s) of WordRep; full dataset coverage and variability across embeddings/tasks not fully reported in-text.
Model is computationally intensive; sensitivity to hyperparameters and vocab intersection choices may affect reproducibility.

supporting_evidence: Proposal defines easily accessible information as "information that model can quickly learn to use."

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If chosen classifiers do not represent practical downstream learners or if their inductive biases mismatch target applications, measured data efficiency may not reflect real-world transferability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: AUC of learning curve is an appropriate summary metric for data efficiency across dataset sizes.
supporting_evidence: Proposal: "A sensible default is to report AUC of learning curve for each task."
Tables 1 and 3 include 'auc rank' as third column.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If AUC weights large- and small-data regimes improperly for a given application, evaluation conclusions (ordering of embeddings) might be misleading for intended use-cases.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The selected datasets (15 datasets across Similarity, Analogy, Sentence, Single word) are representative of common downstream tasks for evaluating embeddings.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If datasets are unrepresentative (e.g., biased toward properties some embeddings capture), conclusions about data efficiency, nonlinear encoding, and ranking stability may not generalize to other tasks/applications.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Intersecting and lowercasing vocabularies and normalizing vectors to unit length does not materially alter comparative evaluation outcomes.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: ANOVA-based pairwise tests on repeated splits are sufficient to determine when embedding scores are 'not significantly different' for ranking.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Experiments §3.3 (lines ~333-342): ranking procedure using pairwise ANOVA

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If ANOVA assumptions (normality, equal variances) are violated for score distributions or if multiple comparisons correction is inadequate, grouping and ranks may be unreliable, affecting reported rank stability and comparisons.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Injective embeddings are common in NLP (finite discrete vocabularies), so preserving information in principle is trivial; practical differences arise from sample complexity and model class.
supporting_evidence: Appendix A: argument that every injective embedding preserves task information and that in discrete/finite NLP settings non-injective embeddings are rare.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If embeddings collapse distinct inputs in practice (due to vocabulary mismatches, low dimension, or preprocessing), then claim that only sample complexity/model class matters may not hold and some embeddings might truly lose task-relevant information.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The set of model classes used (listed classifiers and regressors) adequately captures the distinction between linear vs nonlinear extractability.
supporting_evidence: Models include linear (logistic, linear regression implicitly via cosine/3COSADD), and nonlinear (RF, RBF-SVM, CNN, neural regressors).
Authors use differences between these to indicate nonlinear encoding.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If chosen nonlinear models are not representative (too weak/strong) or if their hyperparameter search is uneven, conclusions about nonlinear encoding could be over- or under-stated.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Repeated random splits (6 repetitions) are sufficient to reduce noise in learning curves for ranking and AUC computations.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Experiments §3.3 (lines ~333-342): "Splits are repeated 6 times in total to reduce noise."
supporting_evidence: Explicit statement of 6 repetitions per task/split.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If variance across splits is larger than captured by six repetitions, statistical comparisons and rank stability conclusions may be underpowered or noisy.

argument_focus: Aligning embedding evaluation with transfer learning by measuring data efficiency (learning curves/AUC).
Using supervised, simple tasks (including supervised similarity/analogy) to probe accessible information.
Including model-class diversity (linear vs nonlinear) to detect nonlinear encoding in embeddings.

Empirical comparison of multiple pretrained embeddings across tasks, dataset sizes, and model classes.
Practical recommendations: report learning curves, AUC, include supervised versions of intrinsic tasks, and diverse classifiers.

Stability of embedding ranks between small-data (30%) and full-data (100%), including mean rank changes and standard deviations (Tables 1 & 3).
Extent to which nonlinear models outperform linear ones per embedding and task (Figure 1; §3.6).

Statistical methods: reliance on pairwise ANOVA for ranking and 6 repetitions may be underpowered for some comparisons; multiple comparison control and ANOVA assumptions are not fully detailed.
Metric choices: AUC as aggregation is proposed but alternatives and sensitivity to weighting across dataset sizes are not explored.

chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should verify preprocessing pipeline: vocab intersection, lowercasing, and unit-normalization — test sensitivity of key claims to these choices (A4).
Recompute results with alternative statistical tests and multiple-comparisons corrections when forming ranks (A5); consider bootstrap confidence intervals for AUC and rank differences.
Check robustness to number of repeated splits and dataset sampling (A8): increase repetitions and report variance of AUC and rank changes.
Assess sensitivity to choice of aggregation metric (A2): compare AUC with other summaries (e.g., initial-slope, performance at fixed small n, weighted AUC emphasizing small-data).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that standard intrinsic evaluations of word embeddings (cosine-based similarity and constant-model analogy tests) poorly reflect embeddings' usefulness for transfer learning. It proposes an evaluation protocol that: (1) measures data efficiency by varying supervised training set size and reporting learning curves (with AUC as a default aggregate); (2) prioritizes simple supervised tasks (single-word classification, supervised similarity/analogy) to probe extractable information; and (3) evaluates a diversity of classifier families (linear and nonlinear) to detect nonlinear encoding. The authors present an empirical study across 15 datasets and multiple pretrained embeddings showing (a) supervised similarity/analogy models can outperform constant baselines, (b) embedding rankings shift when dataset size changes, (c) some embeddings yield better performance with nonlinear models, and (d) single-word properties are quickly learnable. The paper provides theoretical motivation (injective embeddings preserve information but differ in sample complexity) and practical recommendations. Overall the logical chain is plausible and mostly supported by presented experiments, but several inferential steps rely on assumptions or limited experimental coverage (dataset selection, preprocessing choices, statistical testing and aggregation choices).
logical_argument_graph: Premise P1: The primary goal of representation learning (for transfer) is to make subsequent learning faster (lower sample complexity).
Premise P2: Common intrinsic evaluations (cosine similarity, constant-model analogy) assume a fixed recovery model and may miss information that is extractable by supervised learners.

Theoretical observation T1: Injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk; thus differences between embeddings for transfer are about learning difficulty (sample complexity and hypothesis class needed), not absolute information loss.
Inference I1: Therefore, evaluating embeddings for transfer should measure how quickly downstream models can learn (data efficiency) and across model classes (to capture nonlinear encodings).

Proposal S1: Operationalize evaluation by (a) varying supervised dataset size and reporting learning curves; (b) summarizing curves via AUC as a sensible default; (c) including simple supervised tasks and diverse classifiers (linear and nonlinear); (d) include supervised analogs of intrinsic tasks (learnable WS/WA).

Empirical test E1: Run experiments on 15 datasets and multiple pretrained embeddings, using repeated splits (6 repetitions), ANOVA-based pairwise testing for ranking, and a set of classifiers per task.
Empirical findings F1: Supervised similarity/analogy models improve over constant baselines (e.g., ~11% average on tested WordRep subset).
F2: Embedding ranking changes with training set size (mean abs rank change ~0.6), demonstrating data-efficiency differences across embeddings and tasks.
F3: Nonlinear models sometimes outperform linear ones, indicating nonlinear encoding of information in some embeddings (illustrated by normalized differences in Fig.1).
F4: Single-word properties are generally quickly learnable with small data; fitting adds little benefit.

Conclusion C1: The proposed evaluation protocol yields richer, arguably more transfer-relevant diagnostics than standard intrinsic measures and should be adopted (as a sensible default) when transfer is the focus.

Caveat CV1: Generality depends on dataset selection, preprocessing choices (lowercasing, vocab intersection, normalization), statistical choices (ANOVA, 6 repetitions), and aggregation (AUC) — these assumptions can affect conclusions.

identified_claims.claim_text: Current popular evaluation practices for word embeddings (especially unsupervised intrinsic measures like cosine-based similarity and constant-model analogy tests) do not adequately reflect how useful embeddings are for transfer learning.
evidence: Abstract: authors state that information about similarity/analogy tends to be non-linearly encoded, questioning cosine-based unsupervised evaluation.

identified_claims.claim_label: Evaluation should focus on data efficiency
identified_claims.claim_text: Evaluation should emphasize data efficiency: vary available supervised training set size, report learning curves and aggregate measures (e.g., AUC) to reflect how quickly useful information can be extracted from embeddings.

Empirical observation that rankings can change between small and large training sizes (§3.5).

Empirical cases where nonlinear classifiers yield higher scores.

strengths.title: Clear alignment of evaluation with transfer objective
strengths.description: The paper grounds evaluation recommendations in the transfer-learning goal (minimizing sample complexity), connecting theory and practice.
evidence: Proposal articulates that representation learning should make subsequent learning faster and formalizes an expected loss over classifiers and dataset sizes (Eq.1).
Appendix theoretical observation that injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk motivates focusing on learning difficulty.

strengths.title: Operational, actionable protocol
strengths.description: Authors provide a concrete evaluation recipe: vary dataset size, report learning curves/AUC, include supervised versions of intrinsic tasks and diverse model classes.
evidence: Proposal section lists practical steps and default AUC aggregation; Experiments implement these choices across 15 datasets and multiple embeddings.
Appendix B provides implementation details for learnable analogy regressor.

strengths.title: Empirical evidence illustrating claims
strengths.description: The experiments demonstrate concrete phenomena: supervised WS/WA can improve performance, rank changes with data size, and nonlinear models sometimes yield gains.
evidence: §3.4 reported ~11% improvement on WordRep subset using NN regressor; Figures 2-4 and Tables 1 & 3 present concrete comparative results.
Figure 1 quantifies nonlinear vs linear gains per embedding.

strengths.title: Transparency and reproducibility intent
strengths.description: Authors commit to releasing all results and analysis scripts online, enabling verification and further analyses.
evidence: Multiple statements: 'All results and analysis scripts are available online' and 'All results are available online.'

concerns.title: Aggregation choice (AUC) not fully justified or sensitivity-tested
concerns.description: AUC of learning curve is proposed as the default aggregation metric, but the manuscript lacks analysis of how sensitive ranking and conclusions are to this choice (e.g., initial performance, slope, weighted AUC emphasizing small-data).
evidence: Proposal recommends AUC as sensible default but shared analysis notes 'alternative aggregations ... are not compared.'
No ablation comparing AUC to fixed-n performance or initial slope is presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include an ablation comparing AUC with other summary metrics (performance at fixed small n, initial slope, weighted AUC emphasizing small-data) and report how rankings and main conclusions change.

concerns.title: Statistical ranking procedure relies on ANOVA without diagnostics
concerns.description: Embedding ranking uses greedy grouping based on pairwise ANOVA tests across 6 repetitions; manuscript does not report checks of ANOVA assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity), multiple-comparison control, or robustness to number of splits.
evidence: §3.3 describes ranking via pairwise ANOVA but no diagnostics or alternative nonparametric tests are provided.
Shared analysis highlights risk that ANOVA assumptions may be violated and 6 repetitions may be underpowered.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions, apply nonparametric alternatives (e.g., Wilcoxon, permutation tests), correct for multiple comparisons (e.g., Holm/Benjamini–Hochberg), and assess robustness by increasing split repetitions or bootstrap CI for AUC and ranks.

concerns.title: Preprocessing (lowercasing, vocab intersection, normalization) may confound comparisons
concerns.description: All embeddings were lowercased, vocabularies intersected and vectors unit-normalized prior to experiments; these operations can affect embeddings differently (e.g., casing-sensitive embeddings or those using norms), potentially biasing comparative outcomes.
evidence: §3.2 footnote states 'Vocabularies were lowercased and intersected... Vectors were normalized to a unit length.'
Shared analysis flags that preprocessing may change embedding properties non-uniformly.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report sensitivity analyses showing how key results (rank changes, nonlinear gains, supervised WS/WA improvements) vary when (a) not lowercasing, (b) avoiding aggressive vocab intersection, and (c) preserving original norms for embeddings that encode magnitude.

concerns.title: Limited exploration of model families and hyperparameter parity
concerns.description: Conclusions about 'nonlinear encoding' hinge on a particular set of nonlinear models (RF, RBF-SVM, CNN, small NN) and unspecified parity in hyperparameter search; uneven tuning could bias observed nonlinear advantages.
evidence: §3.1 lists models used; §3.6 interprets nonlinear gains as evidence of nonlinear encoding.
Shared analysis notes dependence on model selection and hyperparameter search.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide hyperparameter search budgets per model class, ensure comparable tuning effort across linear and nonlinear models, and consider adding or ablationing alternative nonlinear hypothesis classes (deeper nets, wider kernels, sparsity-inducing linear models) to validate claims.

concerns.title: Dataset representativeness and selection bias
concerns.description: The experiments use 15 datasets spanning four categories; however, representativeness of these datasets for 'common downstream tasks' is assumed but not demonstrated—generalization to other tasks or corpora could be limited.
evidence: SHARED_ANALYSIS assumption A3 flags representativeness as implicit and risky.
Some datasets (WordRep subsets) required specific handling and may be atypical.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss selection criteria and limitations, and where possible add a few additional datasets or task types (e.g., sequence tagging with standard splits, or low-resource tasks) or explicitly bound conclusions to the evaluated task suite.

concerns.title: Reproducibility and computational cost not quantified
concerns.description: The protocol (multiple dataset sizes, model classes, hyperparameter searches, repeated splits) can be computationally expensive; the manuscript does not quantify runtime or provide scripts/instructions for reproduction beyond stating that code will be released.
evidence: Appendix B notes analogy regressor 'very computationally intensive'; proposal suggests running many models and splits but lacks cost estimates.
Statements about code availability promise reproducibility but no timeline or resource guidance is given.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide computational cost estimates (e.g., wall-clock hours per embedding/task on a reference machine), and include scripts/configuration for reproducing main tables and figures.

uncertainty_flags: Generality: experiments cover a limited set of embeddings/datasets; claims may not hold across all embedding types or downstream tasks.
Ranking/stats: ANOVA-based rankings with 6 repetitions may be underpowered; assumptions not diagnosed.
Aggregation: choice of AUC as default is not sensitivity-tested; alternative summaries might yield different orderings.
Preprocessing: lowercasing, vocab intersection, and vector normalization may non-uniformly affect embeddings and thereby the comparisons.
alternative_interpretations: Observed nonlinear model gains could stem from unequal hyperparameter tuning or model capacity mismatches favoring nonlinear models rather than intrinsic nonlinear encoding in embeddings.

Rank changes with dataset size might be driven primarily by label frequency/distributional shifts across splits or by the particular subset sampling strategy, not intrinsic data-efficiency differences.

Supervised WS/WA improvements could reflect that the supervised model is effectively memorizing dataset-specific artifacts (annotation biases or vocabulary idiosyncrasies) rather than revealing generalizable embedding information.
transparency_notes: The authors state they will release code and full results; until release, reproduction of all claims is not independently verifiable.
Key operational choices (hyperparameter search ranges, seeds, exact train/dev/test sizes per split, multiple-comparison corrections) are not fully detailed in the main text and should be provided.
Appendix contains architecture and initialization details for the analogy regressor, which aids reproducibility for that component.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Sparse precedent for operationalizing data-efficiency-centric embedding evaluation in the exact form proposed (AUC over learning curves plus supervised intrinsic tasks). This is plausibly novel; novelty should be treated as a signal for potential impact but not as proof of correctness. Methodological choices require sensitivity analyses to support general adoption.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If alternative aggregation metrics (e.g., performance at fixed small-n or weighted AUC) lead to similar embedding orderings and conclusions, the proposed protocol will be robust and valuable.
If ANOVA-free, bootstrap-based significance yields consistent rank groups, the ranking stability claims hold.
If results are stable under different preprocessing (no lowercasing, no vocab intersection, preserving norms), then comparative claims are not artifacts of preprocessing.
If supervised WS/WA gains generalize across multiple analogy/similarity datasets and survive cross-validation with stricter vocab splits, then learnable intrinsic tasks are broadly useful.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that word-embedding evaluation should be oriented to transfer learning: measure data efficiency via learning curves across varying supervised training sizes, summarize via an aggregate (AUC), use simple supervised tasks (including supervised versions of intrinsic tests like similarity and analogy), and include diverse model classes (linear and nonlinear) to reveal encoding properties. The authors empirically evaluate a set of pretrained embeddings on 15 datasets (Similarity, Analogy, Sentence, Single-word), using multiple classifiers (linear and nonlinear), repeated splits (6 repeats), ANOVA-based rank grouping, and a learnable neural regressor for analogy initialized to reproduce 3COSADD. The proposal emphasizes reporting learning curves, AUC, and model diversity. Important operational choices include lowercasing, vocabulary intersection, L2 normalization of vectors, 6 repetitions, and ANOVA-based grouping for ranking.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that word-embedding evaluation should be reframed around transfer learning utility: specifically, measuring data efficiency (learning curves across varied training sizes, summarized by an AUC-like aggregate) on simple supervised probes and across a diverse set of model classes (linear and nonlinear). The authors motivate this with a theoretical observation (injective embeddings preserve information) and with the claim that extractability under limited data and constrained model classes is the practically relevant quantity. They operationalize the proposal via experiments across 15 datasets (Similarity, Analogy, Sentence, Single-word), several pretrained embeddings, and multiple model classes; report that supervised variants of similarity/analogy can improve performance (e.g., analogy via a regression NN initialized to 3COSADD improves accuracy on tested WordRep subsets), that embedding rankings shift as training data grows, and that nonlinear models sometimes outperform linear ones indicating nonlinear encoding. The contribution is primarily methodological + empirical: proposing a default evaluation protocol and demonstrating via experiments that such a protocol reveals properties missed by standard intrinsic (cosine/constant) metrics. Key uncertainties remain around dataset representativeness, statistical testing choices, preprocessing effects, and robustness to model/hyperparameter decisions.

Operationalization: Create supervised versions of similarity/analogy, use 15 datasets, 6 repeats, multiple classifiers (linear and nonlinear), and several pretrained embeddings.
Empirical finding: Supervised similarity/analogy models can improve absolute performance over constant baselines (e.g., ~11% on tested WordRep subset).
Empirical finding: Embedding ranking can change with available training data (30% vs 100% splits) — demonstrating data-efficiency differences.
Empirical finding: Nonlinear models sometimes outperform linear ones, indicating nonlinear encoding of information in embeddings.
Conclusion: The proposed evaluation produces actionable insights for selection and design of embeddings; recommend adopting data-efficiency-focused supervised probes with model diversity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructed reasoning: The paper argues that the standard intrinsic evaluations (cosine-based similarity, constant-model analogy) do not align with the practical goal of representation learning—making downstream learning fast—because they assume a fixed decoder and ignore how quickly different model classes can extract useful information from embeddings. The authors formalize an evaluation perspective that treats embeddings as transfer objects: one should measure how model performance improves with increasing supervised data (learning curves), summarize data efficiency (they propose AUC), and include simple supervised tasks plus a diversity of model classes (linear and nonlinear). The theoretical Appendix supports focusing on sample complexity/model-class constraints by noting injective embeddings preserve information in principle, so practical differences arise from how easily (with how much data and what models) that information can be extracted. Empirically, across 15 datasets and several pretrained embeddings, they show (a) supervised versions of similarity and analogy yield higher recoverable scores than constant baselines (e.g., a neural regressor improves WordRep subsets by ~11%), (b) embedding rankings shift as training data size changes (nontrivial rank mobility), (c) nonlinear models sometimes extract more information than linear ones indicating nonlinear encoding, and (d) single-word properties are generally quickly recoverable with small data. From the disruptive-novelty lens I treat the relative scarcity of identical prior proposals as a plausible innovation signal: the methodological pivot toward measuring data efficiency (learning curves + AUC) and supervised intrinsic-task variants is coherent and addresses a real gap. However, empirical generality is uncertain because of dataset selection, preprocessing (vocab intersection, lowercasing, normalization), limited repetition, and choice of statistical tests (pairwise ANOVA), which may affect rank stability and significance claims. The paper is thus an intellectually coherent and potentially high-impact proposal that needs stronger robustness checks and clearer statistical justification to make its recommendations prescriptive.
logical_argument_graph: Goal: Representations should make downstream learning faster (transfer learning objective).
Observation: Common intrinsic evaluations assume fixed decoders (e.g., cosine) and thus test only separability by that decoder.
Theoretical claim: Injective embeddings preserve Bayes-optimal information; differences are in extractability (sample complexity and model class).
Proposal: Evaluate embeddings by varying supervised training set size, report learning curves, summarize with AUC, and include simple supervised tasks and diverse model classes.

Operationalization: Run experiments on 15 datasets across Similarity/Analogy/Sentence/Single-word categories; use multiple pretrained embeddings and both linear and nonlinear models; repeat splits 6x; compute ranks via pairwise ANOVA.
Empirical findings: Supervised similarity/analogy outperform constant baselines; ranks shift with data size; nonlinear models can outperform linear ones; single-word properties are data-efficient.

Conclusion: Data-efficiency-focused, supervised, model-diverse evaluation yields different and more transfer-relevant insights than standard intrinsic metrics; recommend reporting learning curves/AUC and diverse models.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes reframing word-embedding evaluation around transfer learning utility by measuring data efficiency: report learning curves across varying supervised training sizes, summarize via an aggregate (recommended default: area under the learning curve), prioritize simple supervised probes (single-word classification, supervised similarity/analogy), and evaluate a diverse set of model classes (linear and nonlinear). The empirical study applies this protocol to multiple pretrained embeddings across 15 datasets (Similarity, Analogy, Sentence, Single-word), using several classifiers (linear and nonlinear), repeated random splits (6 repeats), and an ANOVA-based ranking/grouping procedure. Main empirical observations reported: (1) supervised variants of similarity/analogy improve on constant unsupervised baselines (e.g., an analogy regression NN initialized to 3COSADD improved accuracy ~11% on tested WordRep subsets); (2) embedding rankings shift as dataset size increases (mean absolute rank change ~0.6); (3) nonlinear models sometimes outperform linear ones, implying some information is nonlinearly encoded; (4) single-word properties are generally quickly learnable, with small changes from fitting. The paper gives a theoretical justification (injective embeddings preserve information so practical differences are sample-complexity and model-class dependent) and recommends reporting learning curves/AUC and including supervised intrinsic-task variants. Empirical evidence in the manuscript supports these claims for the tested embeddings/datasets, but several inferential steps depend on operational choices (preprocessing, dataset selection, model/hyperparameter search budgets, aggregation choice, and statistical procedures). I flag these dependencies, propose concrete robustness checks, and outline alternative interpretations and uncertainty sources.

Premise: Standard intrinsic evaluations (cosine-based similarity, constant-model analogy) assume fixed decoders and can miss extractable information that requires fitting or nonlinear decoders.
Observation/Theory: Injective embeddings preserve information in principle; differences in practice arise from sample complexity and model class.

Proposal: Evaluate embeddings by measuring data efficiency via learning curves over varying supervised training sizes, summarize (e.g., AUC), use simple supervised probes and a diversity of model classes.

Empirical instantiation: Run experiments on 15 datasets with multiple pretrained embeddings and model classes, repeat splits, compute ranks via ANOVA-based grouping, and compare constant vs supervised variants for intrinsic tasks.

Empirical findings: Supervised similarity/analogy models improve on constant baselines; embedding rankings shift with data size; nonlinear models sometimes outperform linear ones; single-word tasks are quickly learnable.

Conclusion: The proposed evaluation yields actionable insights about embeddings' transfer usefulness and should be adopted as a sensible default, with caveats about dataset/task alignment and methodological robustness.

Shared analysis notes risk A4: preprocessing may confound results.

concerns.title: Aggregation choice (AUC) not sensitivity-tested
concerns.description: AUC of the learning curve is proposed as a default aggregator for data efficiency, but no experiments compare AUC with other summaries (initial-slope, fixed small-n performance, weighted AUC emphasizing small-data) to show robustness of ordering and practical relevance.

Shared analysis flags lack of sensitivity analysis for aggregation (A2).

concerns.description: Ranks are computed by a greedy grouping based on pairwise ANOVA over 6 repeated splits; ANOVA assumptions (normality, equal variances) and multiple-comparisons control are not detailed. Six repetitions may be insufficient for stable inference on some tasks.
evidence: Experiments §3.3: "assign embeddings the same rank if their scores ... are not significantly different, as tested using pairwise ANOVA test. Splits are repeated 6 times."
Shared analysis and prior-stage digests repeatedly flagged A5/A8 concerns about ANOVA and 6 repeats.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions (e.g., residual QQ plots), apply nonparametric alternatives (bootstrap, permutation tests) and correct for multiple comparisons (e.g., Holm/Benjamini-Hochberg), and increase repetitions or provide confidence intervals for AUC/rank differences.

counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If preprocessing choices (lowercasing, vocab intersection, normalization) are shown to have minimal differential effect across embeddings, then the protocol's comparative outcomes are reliable.
If AUC and alternate aggregations yield consistent ordering and conclusions, then the proposed aggregation is robust and suitable as a default.
If nonlinearity findings persist under parity hyperparameter tuning across expanded model families and deeper neural architectures, then the claim of nonlinear encoding is strengthened.
If increased repetitions and nonparametric statistical testing preserve rank-group conclusions, then the ranking/stability claims are statistically sound.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper refines evaluation practice by operationalizing a data-efficiency-centered protocol; this builds on existing concerns about intrinsic evaluations while adding concrete experimental instantiation.
evidence: Proposal section and Eq. (1) formalize the transfer-oriented objective; experiments demonstrate insights (supervised intrinsic tasks, rank mobility).
uncertainty_flags: Empirical robustness to preprocessing, aggregation, and statistical choices remains to be validated.

novelty_lenses.verdict: plausible innovation signal but needs stronger validation
novelty_lenses.rationale: Shifting the canonical default of embedding evaluation away from static intrinsic metrics to transfer-aligned learning-curve reporting is a potentially disruptive methodological change with practical implications.
evidence: Authors show concrete examples where supervised fitting and data-size variation change conclusions drawn about embeddings (e.g., GloVe100 vs GloVe300, NN analogy improvement).
uncertainty_flags: Adoption hinges on computational feasibility, standardization of aggregation/statistical procedures, and robustness across broader tasks and preprocessing variants.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence expresses the reviewer’s belief that the paper's central descriptive claims (that data-efficiency evaluation reveals additional, practically relevant differences among embeddings and that supervised intrinsic-task variants can outperform constant baselines in the tested settings) are well supported for the reported experiments (~high). Lower confidence bounds reflect uncertainty about generalization to other datasets, preprocessing sensitivity, statistical reliability of ranking, and dependence on modeling/hyperparameter choices; these require the robustness checks suggested above.

consensus_findings: Reframing embedding evaluation toward transfer usefulness (measuring data efficiency via learning curves across varying supervised training sizes) is conceptually coherent and aligns evaluation with practical downstream objectives.

Including supervised, simple probes (e.g., supervised variants of similarity and analogy) and testing multiple model classes (linear and nonlinear) can reveal information extractability that static intrinsic measures (cosine, constant analogy heuristics) may miss.

Empirical instantiation across the provided 15 datasets demonstrates phenomena of practical interest: supervised similarity/analogy models can improve over constant baselines in the tested subsets (example: neural regressor improved WordRep subsets by ~11%), embedding rankings can shift with available training data, nonlinear classifiers sometimes outperform linear ones for certain embeddings/tasks, and many single-word properties are recoverable with small amounts of data.

Theoretical motivation (appendix observation: injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk) supports focusing on sample complexity and model-class extractability rather than absolute information loss in finite/discrete vocabularies.

The manuscript offers a concrete, operational evaluation protocol (vary dataset size, report learning curves, aggregate via AUC as a default, include diverse classifiers) that is actionable for practitioners.
disagreements: Severity and practical significance of observed rank changes: some reviewers interpret the reported mean rank change (~0.6) as modest and question practical impact, while others view any rank mobility across data regimes as meaningful evidence that rankings depend on data efficiency.

Novelty magnitude: some assess the proposal as a useful incremental methodological synthesis of prior critiques of intrinsic evaluation; others treat it as a more disruptive reframing with potential to alter standard benchmarking practice.

Sufficiency of experimental coverage: reviewers disagree on whether the 15 datasets and selected embeddings provide adequate generality. Some find the empirical evidence persuasive for the claims as demonstrated; others consider dataset selection and subset usage (e.g., WordRep subsets) insufficient to claim broad generality.

Adequacy of model-family selection and hyperparameter tuning parity: some reviewers accept the chosen model suite as representative for demonstrating nonlinear extractability; others argue the limited nonlinear families and underspecified tuning budgets could explain observed nonlinear gains and thus demand stronger controls.
uncertainty_hotspots: Preprocessing effects: universal lowercasing, vocabulary intersection, and unit-normalization may differentially affect embeddings and could confound relative comparisons (which embeddings lose tokens or rely on case/norm information?).

Statistical ranking and significance testing: reliance on greedy pairwise ANOVA grouping with only six repeated splits raises concerns about ANOVA assumption violations, multiple-comparison control, and underpowered variance estimates for AUC/rank stability.

AUC aggregation choice: AUC of learning curves is proposed as a 'sensible default' but sensitivity to alternative summaries (performance at small fixed n, initial slope, weighted AUC emphasizing small-data) is untested and could change practical conclusions and rankings.

Model-family and hyperparameter parity: the set of nonlinear models evaluated is limited and hyperparameter search procedures and budgets are not fully specified; unequal tuning could cause apparent nonlinear advantages.

Dataset representativeness and scope: results are demonstrated on a specific suite (15 datasets, some analogy/similarity subsets); extrapolation to other tasks, languages, rarer labels, and full analogy datasets remains uncertain.
Repetition/sample variance: six repetitions per split may be insufficient for stable AUC estimates and reliable statistical comparisons on some datasets, especially small or high-variance ones.
model_diversity_effects: Including multiple model classes (linear and nonlinear) revealed that some embedding-task pairs yield measurably better performance with nonlinear learners, indicating that extractable information is sometimes encoded nonlinearly and that single-model (cosine/linear) probes can under-report usable structure.

Model diversity interacts with data size: some embeddings favored by linear models in tiny-data regimes can be overtaken by other embeddings when nonlinear models and more data are available, producing rank mobility across the learning curve.

Observed nonlinear wins are model- and tuning-dependent: without documented parity in hyperparameter search and additional nonlinear families (deeper nets, kernelized linear models), it's unclear whether the effect is attributable to embedding structure or to model capacity/tuning differences.

Practically, model diversity increases diagnostic power (it discriminates whether an embedding's information is linearly or nonlinearly accessible), but it also increases computational cost and demands standardized tuning protocols to produce fair comparisons.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center decisions on whether the contribution advances methodological practice and whether the empirical demonstrations are sufficiently robust to support the recommendations. Key validation items to request from authors before further editorial escalation: (1) robustness analyses for preprocessing choices (lowercasing, vocab intersection, vector normalization) showing how many tokens were dropped per embedding and how main conclusions (rank changes, supervised WS/WA gains, nonlinear advantages) vary without such preprocessing; (2) statistical robustness: diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions, application of nonparametric alternatives (permutation/bootstrap), multiple-comparisons correction, and confidence intervals for AUC and rank differences; (3) sensitivity of aggregation: comparisons between AUC and at least one or two alternative summaries (fixed small-n performance and initial slope or weighted AUC) with effect on rankings reported; (4) model/hyperparameter parity: detailed hyperparameter search spaces and budgets per model class, plus a parity statement and/or additional experiments ensuring nonlinear advantages persist under balanced tuning; (5) targeted extensions to the empirical coverage: either expand supervised analogy/similarity experiments to more categories/benchmarks or clearly qualify claims as limited to the evaluated suite. If authors supply these robustness checks and clarifications, the manuscript's methodological proposal will be much better grounded for community adoption.
meta_review.author_guidance: Address the main uncertainty hotspots with targeted reproducibility and sensitivity analyses: (1) Preprocessing ablations: report per-embedding vocabulary coverage before/after intersection, runs without lowercasing and without unit-normalization for a representative subset of tasks/embeddings, and show how rankings/AUCs change; (2) Statistical rigor: provide diagnostic plots for ANOVA residuals, report results from nonparametric tests (permutation or Wilcoxon) and bootstrap CIs for AUC and rank differences, and state and apply multiple-comparisons corrections used in ranking; (3) Aggregation sensitivity: include comparisons of AUC with alternative summaries (performance at small fixed n, initial slope, and a weighted-AUC emphasizing small-data) and discuss when each summary is preferable for different application priorities; (4) Model tuning transparency: publish hyperparameter search spaces, selection criteria, and compute budgets; ensure comparable tuning effort across linear and nonlinear model classes and add ablations that hold capacity or regularization constant to test nonlinearity claims; (5) Empirical breadth: either extend supervised similarity/analogy experiments to additional datasets (or full WordRep/google/msr if feasible) or clearly delimit the scope of empirical claims; (6) Repetition and variance: increase repetitions or apply bootstrap across training-set draws for a representative subset to quantify variability and report CIs; (7) Reproducibility artifacts: release code, exact preprocessing scripts, random seeds, per-run logs, and compute/time estimates to facilitate independent validation. In the text, temper universal claims and explicitly report limitations where robustness checks leave residual uncertainty.
transparency_report: Authors state intent to release all results and analysis scripts online; Appendix contains architecture and initialization details for the analogy regressor, which aids reproducibility for that component.

Operational choices are partially reported (datasets, model classes, preprocessing note: lowercasing, vocab intersection, L2 normalization, six repeats, greedy ANOVA grouping) but several important procedural details are missing or underspecified in the current manuscript: exact hyperparameter search spaces and budgets per model class, seeds and exact split sizes, diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions and multiple-comparisons correction, counts of tokens removed by vocabulary intersection per embedding, and compute/runtime estimates.

Until the promised code and full logs (preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning logs, per-split metrics) are available, independent verification of some claims (especially those sensitive to preprocessing or tuning) will be limited.
epistemic_limits: The assessment is constrained by (1) reliance on reviewers' reading of the provided manuscript extracts rather than running the experiments; claims about robustness depend on analyses the authors have not yet provided (preprocessing ablations, alternative aggregations, nonparametric statistical tests, expanded repetitions), (2) the finite empirical coverage in the manuscript (a particular set of pretrained embeddings and 15 datasets, with some analogy/similarity subsets), which limits generalization to other embeddings, tasks, languages, and low-resource regimes, and (3) unspecified hyperparameter-search details and compute budgets that make it difficult to disentangle whether observed nonlinear advantages reflect embedding encoding or model/tuning artifacts. Where reviewers flagged issues, these reflect plausible alternative explanations rather than proven refutations; the recommended robustness checks would reduce these epistemic uncertainties.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes reframing word-embedding evaluation toward transfer utility by measuring data efficiency: report learning curves across varied supervised training sizes, summarize with an aggregate (recommended default: AUC), include supervised variants of intrinsic tasks (similarity/analogy), and evaluate a diversity of model classes (linear and nonlinear). Empirical results on a suite of 15 datasets and multiple pretrained embeddings show supervised similarity/analogy often improve over constant baselines (example: a neural regressor improved selected WordRep subsets by ~11%), embedding rankings can shift with available labeled data, nonlinear models sometimes outperform linear ones (indicating nonlinearly encoded information), and many single-word properties are quickly recoverable with little data. The appendix gives a simple theoretical motivation (injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk), justifying focus on sample complexity and model-class extractability rather than absolute information loss.
strengths: Clear reframing: Aligns embedding evaluation with practical transfer-learning objectives (sample complexity/data efficiency) and gives a coherent formalization (Eq.1) tying tasks, classifiers, and dataset-size distributions together.

Operational protocol: Provides an actionable evaluation recipe (learning curves across dataset sizes, AUC aggregation as default, supervised intrinsic-task variants, and model-class diversity) and implements it empirically across many datasets and embeddings.

Empirical illustrations: Demonstrates concrete phenomena of interest (supervised WS/WA gains, rank mobility across data regimes, nonlinear-vs-linear differences, quick recoverability of single-word properties) that intrinsic static probes can miss.
Reproducibility intent and partial detail: Appendix gives architecture/initialization details for the analogy regressor and the authors state they will release code and full results.
limitations: Preprocessing confound: All experiments use universal lowercasing, vocabulary intersection, and unit-normalization of vectors. These operations can differentially affect embeddings (e.g., case-sensitive models or those using norm magnitude), and the manuscript does not report per-embedding token-loss statistics or ablations showing sensitivity of key claims to these preprocessing choices.

Statistical-rigor and ranking methodology under-specified: Embedding ranks are formed by greedy pairwise ANOVA across only six repeated splits. The paper lacks diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions (normality/homoscedasticity), explicit multiple-comparison control, bootstrap/permutation tests, or confidence intervals for AUC and rank differences — all of which could materially affect significance/rank-group assignments.

Aggregation-choice sensitivity untested: AUC of the learning curve is proposed as a sensible default but no ablation compares it to alternative summaries that emphasize tiny-data regimes (e.g., performance at fixed small n, initial slope, weighted-AUC). Rankings and practical decisions may change with aggregation choice.

Model-family and hyperparameter-parity ambiguity: The claim that some information is nonlinearly encoded relies on comparisons between limited nonlinear families and linear baselines, but hyperparameter searchspaces, budgets, and parity across model classes are not fully documented; uneven tuning could explain apparent nonlinear advantages.
open_questions: Please provide preprocessing sensitivity results: how many vocabulary tokens per embedding were removed by intersection/lowercasing, and how do core outcomes (AUC ranks, supervised WS/WA gains, nonlinear vs linear differences) change if (a) lowercasing is not applied, (b) vocabularies are not intersected, and (c) original vector norms are preserved?

Please strengthen statistical inference: supply diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions, apply and report nonparametric alternatives (permutation tests or bootstrap CIs) for AUC and rank differences, and state/use multiple-comparisons corrections. How do ranking/grouping outcomes change under these more robust tests?

Provide aggregation-sensitivity analysis: compare AUC ranking with at least two alternative summaries (e.g., performance at fixed small-n, initial slope between small-n points, and a weighted-AUC emphasizing small-data). Do the main qualitative conclusions and embedding orderings persist?

Clarify hyperparameter search and tuning parity: report search spaces, budgets, validation procedures, and whether tuning effort was balanced across linear and nonlinear model classes. In parity-controlled ablations, do nonlinear advantages remain?

Scope/generalization: Can the authors expand supervised WS/WA experiments beyond the tested WordRep subsets (or justify subset use) and/or include one or two additional downstream tasks (e.g., tagging/NER or domain-shifted low-resource tasks) to show generality of data-efficiency signals?
consensus_snapshot: Evaluating embeddings by measuring how quickly downstream supervised models learn (learning curves across dataset sizes) is a conceptually appropriate and useful reframing for transfer-focused evaluation.

Including supervised variants of intrinsic tasks (learnable similarity/analogy) and multiple model classes (linear and nonlinear) provides additional, practical diagnostic information relative to static intrinsic metrics (cosine, constant analogy heuristics).
The appendix theoretical point (injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk) gives a sound motivation for focusing on sample complexity and model-class extractability.
The empirical study reveals informative behaviors (supervised WS/WA gains, rank mobility, nonlinear wins, easy single-word tasks) on the evaluated dataset/embedding suite.
disagreement_snapshot: Magnitude and practical significance of reported rank mobility: some reviewers find the mean rank change (~0.6) modest and question its practical import, while others treat even moderate mobility as evidence that simple intrinsic rankings can be misleading across data budgets.

Novelty assessment: reviewers vary between viewing the work as a useful incremental operationalization and viewing it as a potentially disruptive reframing; opinions differ on how novel the exact combination (learning curves + supervised intrinsic probes + AUC + model diversity) is relative to prior critique literature.

Sufficiency of experimental coverage: there is disagreement on whether 15 datasets (with some analogy/similarity subsets) suffice to generalize conclusions; some reviewers request broader task inclusion or stronger qualification of general claims.

Adequacy of model/hyperparameter treatment: while some accept the chosen model suite as illustrative, others demand clearer parity in hyperparameter search to rule out tuning-induced nonlinear advantages.
uncertainty_snapshot: Preprocessing impact: extent to which lowercasing, vocab intersection, and normalization changed embedding-specific signals is unknown and could materially alter comparative conclusions.
Ranking/statistical reliability: ANOVA-based grouping with six repeats may be underpowered or violate assumptions, introducing uncertainty in reported ranks and stability claims.
Aggregation choice: sensitivity of conclusions to using AUC as the default aggregator is untested; alternative summaries might reorder embeddings for small-data-focused applications.
Model/tuning confounds: whether nonlinear wins reflect embedding structure or uneven model capacity/tuning is unresolved pending parity analyses.
Generality: extrapolation to other embeddings, languages, or downstream tasks remains uncertain until additional datasets and full-set analyses are reported.

(6) Reproducibility: release code, seeds, per-run logs, and compute/time estimates. Revise claims to reflect robustness boundaries revealed by these checks.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The manuscript gives a coherent and actionable proposal to evaluate word embeddings by their transfer usefulness: measure data efficiency via learning curves across supervised dataset sizes, summarize with an aggregate (AUC as a sensible default), include supervised variants of intrinsic tasks (similarity/analogy), and compare across diverse model classes. Empirical work across 15 datasets and several pretrained embeddings demonstrates that supervised probes can improve over constant intrinsic baselines, that embedding rankings can change with data budget, that nonlinear models sometimes extract more information than linear ones, and that single-word properties are often quickly learnable.

Strengths: The proposal aligns evaluation with practical transfer objectives and formalizes the idea (Eq.1). It is operational and implemented across multiple datasets/embeddings. Empirical findings concretely illustrate behaviors that would be invisible to static intrinsic metrics. Theoretical appendix clarifies the motivation (injectivity => preserved Bayes risk; differences are extractability/sample complexity).

Limitations: First, preprocessing choices (lowercasing, vocabulary intersection, unit-normalization) are applied universally but not ablated; these could differentially affect embeddings and bias comparisons. Second, the ranking/statistical procedure (greedy pairwise ANOVA with six repetitions) is under-specified: diagnostic checks for ANOVA assumptions, multiple-comparisons control, and nonparametric/bootstrapped CIs are absent, leaving rank/group assignments and reported stability uncertain. Third, AUC is proposed without sensitivity analysis vs alternatives that emphasize tiny-data regimes—different summaries may yield different practical orderings. Fourth, the claim of nonlinear encoding depends on model family selection and undisclosed tuning parity; uneven hyperparameter search could explain nonlinear gains.

Open Questions: (1) Provide per-embedding vocabulary coverage statistics and ablations for preprocessing variations (no-lowercasing, no-intersection, original norms) — do core results persist? (2) Report diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions and complementary nonparametric or bootstrap-based inference (CIs, permutation tests); how do ranks change under these tests? (3) Compare AUC with at least two alternative aggregation summaries (fixed small-n performance, initial slope, or weighted-AUC); are conclusions stable? (4) Publish hyperparameter search spaces and budgets per model class and demonstrate tuning parity; under parity, do nonlinear wins persist? (5) Clarify scope: can supervised similarity/analogy gains be reproduced across more analogy/similarity categories or full datasets, or should claims be limited to the tested subsets?

Transparency: The manuscript promises code and full results and includes some architecture detail (Appendix B). To enable independent verification, the released artifacts should include preprocessing scripts, per-embedding token-loss counts, hyperparameter search logs and budgets, seed/split definitions, per-run outputs for all repetitions, statistical-test code, and compute/time estimates. Without these, key claims (preprocessing-insensitive rank mobility, nonlinear encoding) remain partially unverifiable.

Overall: The manuscript advances a useful, practically motivated evaluation protocol that is likely to be valuable to the community if its robustness is established. The next step is to provide the targeted sensitivity and statistical robustness analyses requested above so readers can judge which findings are stable and in which contexts the proposed defaults (AUC, model families, supervised intrinsic probes) should be adopted.

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects substantive methodological uncertainties (preprocessing sensitivity, statistical testing, aggregation choice, and model-tuning parity) that could alter some conclusions; upper bound reflects consistency of conceptual framing, coherent theoretical motivation, and empirical illustrations across many datasets that support the central proposal. Supplying the requested robustness analyses would narrow uncertainty and move confidence toward the upper bound.
